I found the cause of the pause but have not changed anything yet. I need your decision on which fix to make.

**What happened**
- SABnzbd paused 4 times: Oct 31, and Nov 4 at 14:10, 18:13 and 22:14. It stayed paused until you resumed it at 20:11 today.
- The last pause came after the pod restarted on Nov 4 at 21:38. So the fix did not stop it.
- Every pause has the same cause. SABnzbd gets `BlockingIOError [Errno 11]` or `ConnectionAbortedError [Errno 103]` at `os.close(fd)` while it assembles a file in `/downloads/incomplete`. It then reports "Disk error" and pauses.
- This is the SMB client failing to flush a cached write when the file closes. The mount uses `cache=strict`.
- The node kernel log (`k8s-3`) shows no CIFS errors at the pause times. The log may have rolled over.

**What I could not find**
- The repo has no SMB fix. The mount options in `pvs.yaml` and `storageclass.yaml` have not changed since May 30.
- The live PV matches the repo. Tell me which fix you mean if it was something else, such as a node change.

**Fix options**
1. Move `/downloads/incomplete` to a Longhorn PVC and keep only `complete` on SMB. SABnzbd writes thousands of small chunks to `incomplete`, so this takes the heavy write load off SMB. I recommend this one.
2. Change `cache=strict` to `cache=none` on the downloads PV. This is a smaller change, but writes get slower and it may not fully stop the errors.

Yes, both are possible, but only over SSH. I have not seen your NAS internals yet, so a few parts are untested.

## Temperature
You can get this without extra software on the NAS.
- **Drive temperature:** `smartctl_exporter` exports each drive's SMART temperature. The unas-pro-tools README does not say so, but this is a standard `smartctl` metric.
- **CPU and board temperature:** `node_exporter` has a `hwmon` collector. It exports the sensors under `/sys/class/hwmon`. I do not know which sensors the UNAS exposes. I will find out once I have SSH access.
- **Fan speed:** The same `hwmon` collector may show it.

## SMB metrics
The [KPN thread](https://community.kpn.com/thuisnetwerk-72/linux-cifs-smb-loopt-vast-bij-langdurige-schrijfacties-naar-unas-pro-d-state-cifs-vfs-timeout-650815) mentions `smbd`, so the UNAS appears to run Samba. I cannot confirm that until I log in. There are two ways to get the data:

1. **A small script (my pick).** It runs `smbstatus` every 15 seconds and writes a file for the `node_exporter` textfile collector. It exports these values:
   - Number of sessions.
   - Number of open files and locks.
   - Memory use and CPU of the `smbd` processes. Memory is the main suspect.
   - Free RAM on the NAS.

   This is about 20 lines of shell. It adds no new software, and I can write it to the same `/persistent/` folder.
2. **[`samba_exporter`](https://github.com/imker25/samba_exporter).** It reads `smbstatus` and procfs and serves metrics on port 9922. It has a more complete metric set, but it ships as DEB and RPM packages only, and I could not confirm its metric names. It is a heavier install on a locked-down appliance.

The Samba logs on the NAS are not a metric. They may still show why a session dropped. I can look at them by hand once I have SSH.

Yes. I read the NAS logs first, and they show the real cause of the pauses.

## The finding
Every SABnzbd pause matches a Samba session reset on the NAS. The NAS journal logs a disconnect of the shares from `k8s-3` at each time:

| SABnzbd paused | NAS logged disconnect |
|---|---|
| Oct 31 21:18 | Oct 31 21:17 and 21:18 |
| Nov 4 14:10 | Nov 4 14:10 |
| Nov 4 18:13 | Nov 4 18:13 |
| Nov 4 22:14 | Nov 4 22:14:15 (pause at 22:14:17) |

- At 22:14:15 all three shares (`IPC$`, `Config`, `Media`) disconnected. The client reconnected in the same second with a new login. That cuts off the writes that were in flight.
- The NAS network link did not drop at these times. The link flaps on Oct 30 and Nov 8 do not match. The Nov 8 flaps also reset the session (00:57), but SABnzbd was not writing then.
- The same journal shows 20 Samba lock errors (`NT_STATUS_NOT_LOCKED` in `g_lock_writev_data`). The 22:18 error came 4 minutes after the reset. I have not yet linked these errors to the resets.
- The disconnects at 19:39, 20:13, 20:57, 21:00 and 21:32 on Nov 4 did not cause a pause. They happened while few writes were in progress.

I do not know yet which side closes the session, the client or `smbd`. Logs from both sides at the same moment will show it.

## Log shipping plan
The NAS has `journald`, which holds `smbd`, `smbd_audit`, kernel and `earlyoom` messages. The cluster already has Loki and Alloy.
1. **On the NAS:** Run Grafana Alloy (arm64) from `/persistent/`. It reads the journal and the Samba logs and pushes them to Loki. It uses the same restore script as the metrics tools.
2. **In the cluster:** Loki is only reachable inside the cluster now. I add an `HTTPRoute` on `envoy-internal` (`10.20.0.3`, LAN only). The Loki push endpoint has no login, so only your LAN can use it.
3. **Label and dashboard:** Logs get the label `host=nas`. I add a Grafana panel that shows NAS SMB disconnects next to the SABnzbd pause times. This needs the cluster-side `k8s-3` kernel logs too. Alloy in the cluster may already collect those.

I found four gaps on `k8s-3`. The first is the most important.

| Priority | Gap | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **No CIFS client metrics.** `node_cifs_*` does not exist. | Reconnect counts live in `/proc/fs/cifs/Stats` and `DebugData`. I read them by hand earlier: 35 session and 99 share reconnects since boot. Without a graph, I cannot see when they happen. |

| 3 | **No SABnzbd state metric or alert.** | The pause lasted 5 days before you noticed. There is no `paused` metric and no alert. |
| 4 | **No dashboard** for NAS or SMB. | The data exists, but nothing shows it side by side. |

**What is already covered**
- `node-exporter` runs on `k8s-3` and `pop-os`. It gives TCP retransmits (1.19 M) and timeouts (119), memory and I/O pressure, conntrack, and softnet drops (0).
- Cilium drop counts, container CPU and restart counts also exist.
- The 800,702 dropped-packet figure is the NAS network card, not `k8s-3`.

**Proposed fixes**
1. **CIFS metrics:** A small DaemonSet reads `/proc/fs/cifs/Stats` every 15 seconds and writes a `.prom` file. `node-exporter` serves it through its textfile collector. Any pod can read this `/proc` path, because I read it from the SABnzbd pod. The metrics would be reconnect counts, failed operations, and open files.
2. **Node logs:** Talos can send its kernel and service logs to a TCP or UDP address (`machine.logging` and the kernel argument `talos.logging.kernel`). Alloy needs a receiver for this. It needs a Talos config change on each node, so it needs a node apply. I would test it on `k8s-3` first.
3. **SABnzbd:** Add a `sabnzbd_exporter` with a `VMServiceScrape`, plus a `VMRule` alert when the queue is paused for more than 5 minutes.
4. **Dashboard:** One Grafana dashboard with the SMB disconnect log lines, CIFS reconnects, NAS network drops, NAS temperatures, and the SABnzbd paused state.

**One finding about the cause.** The `k8s-3` kernel log has no CIFS error at the Nov 4 22:14 reset. A client timeout normally prints "has not responded in 180 seconds". So the client did not time out. The reset is more likely from the NAS side or the network between the two. This is a guess and not proof, because the CIFS client logs little by default.

apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: KmsgLogConfig
name: remote-log
url: tcp://host:5044/

machine:

Service log messages always include `msg`, `talos-level`, `talos-service`, and `talos-time`. Additional fields may also appear, and any `extraTags` are added to every message.

**Yes, it exists, but it's experimental.** `otelcol.receiver.tcplog` accepts log messages over TCP and forwards them to other `otelcol.*` components. It wraps the upstream OpenTelemetry `tcplog` receiver. You must set the `stability.level` flag to `experimental` to use it. The docs warn that experimental components "are subject to frequent breaking changes."

**Minimal example** (based on the page's example):

```alloy
otelcol.receiver.tcplog "default" {
  listen_address = "localhost:1515"
  output {
    logs = [otelcol.exporter.debug.default.input]
  }
}

otelcol.exporter.debug "default" {}
```

**Supported arguments:**

- `listen_address` (required): the host:port to listen on.
- `add_attributes`: adds `net.*` attributes following OpenTelemetry semantic conventions (default `false`).
- `auth`: an `otelcol.auth` handler that authenticates each TCP connection.
- `encoding`: one of `utf-8`, `utf-16le`, `utf-16be`, `ascii`, `big5`, or `nop` (default `"utf-8"`).
- `max_log_size`: maximum size of a log entry, with a minimum of `64KiB` (default `"1MiB"`).
- `one_log_per_packet`: skips log tokenization when each message is one log and multiline isn't used (default `false`).

**Blocks:** `output` (required), `multiline`, `retry_on_failure`, `tls`, `tpm`, and `debug_metrics`.

**JSON parsing:** The page doesn't document operators or parsers, so there's no JSON parsing option here. The closest options are `multiline` for splitting entries and `encoding` for character sets.

**Loki conversion:** The page doesn't cover `otelcol.exporter.loki` or attribute-to-label mapping. To wire this receiver to Loki, you'll need that exporter's documentation. The only connection this page documents is the `output.logs` list, which accepts OpenTelemetry consumers.

  name: alloy-node-logs
spec:

    spec:
      chart: alloy
      version: 1.15.0
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: grafana
  interval: 1h
  values:
    controller:
      type: daemonset
      hostNetwork: true # Talos can only reach 127.0.0.1 on the host
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet
    alloy:

      extraArgs:
        - --stability.level=experimental
      extraEnv:
        - name: NODE_NAME

            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: spec.nodeName
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 20m
        limits:
          memory: 256Mi
      configMap:
        content: |
          otelcol.receiver.tcplog "talos" {
            listen_address = "127.0.0.1:6050"
            output {
              logs = [otelcol.exporter.loki.talos.input]
            }
          }

          otelcol.exporter.loki "talos" {
            forward_to = [loki.process.talos.receiver]
          }

          // Kernel lines carry no talos-service, so the service label is only set for service logs.
          loki.process "talos" {
            stage.json {
              expressions = {level = "\"talos-level\"", service = "\"talos-service\""}

            stage.labels {
              values = {level = "", service = ""}

            stage.static_labels {
              values = {job = "talos", node = sys.env("NODE_NAME")}
            }
            forward_to = [loki.write.endpoint.receiver]

            endpoint {

## What I built

**Item 2: node logs**
- **Alloy receiver:** `alloy/app/helmrelease-node-logs.yaml` adds a third Alloy release, `alloy-node-logs`. It runs on the host network and listens on `127.0.0.1:6050`. It sends the lines to Loki with the labels `job=talos`, `node`, `level` and `service`. It uses `otelcol.receiver.tcplog`, which is experimental in Alloy. It could break on an Alloy upgrade.
- **Talos patch:** `talos/patches/global/machine-logging.yaml` sends service logs and kernel logs (`KmsgLogConfig`) to that address. `talhelper genconfig --dry-run` shows only added lines. The patch applies without a reboot.

**Item 3: SABnzbd**
- **Exporter and scrape:** `exportarr` v2.3.0 runs as a second container in the SABnzbd pod. A `ServiceMonitor` scrapes it. It reads the API key from `app-secrets`.
- **Alerts:** `vmrule.yaml` alerts when `sabnzbd_paused` stays at 1 for 5 minutes. A second alert fires if the exporter cannot read the SABnzbd API.
- **Checks:** The Helm render and the server-side dry run both pass.

## Would NFS fix this?
It might, but a cheaper test comes first.
- Your pauses are errors returned to SABnzbd (`EAGAIN`, `ECONNABORTED`) when an SMB session resets. Your mount uses `soft`. That is the CIFS default, and it returns errors on a reset. A `hard` mount keeps retrying and replays the operation after the reconnect, so SABnzbd would see a short stall and no error. I have not tested this.
- The UNAS Pro supports NFS. You turn it on in UniFi Drive under Settings, then Services ([Ubiquiti guide](https://help.ui.com/hc/en-us/articles/REDACTED)). NFS mounts are `hard` by default, so it would also survive a reset. It has no sessions, and it avoids the Samba lock errors I saw. But it needs a new CSI driver, PVs for all shares, and permission changes (`uid`/`gid` mapping).
- The root cause is still unknown. A reset could hit NFS too, as a stall.

I suggest trying `hard` on the `media-downloads` PV first. It is one line. If pauses continue, move `incomplete` to Longhorn or try NFS.

Setting `hard` on the SABnzbd volume takes two steps. The server accepts the change to the live PV (I tested with a dry run).

**1. Change the PV in git**
- The file is `kubernetes/apps/default/storage/app/pvs.yaml`. Add `- hard` to the `mountOptions` list of `media-downloads` (line 141 onward).
- I suggest only that PV. The pauses come from writes to `/downloads`, and a `hard` mount can freeze a pod if the NAS goes away.
- A StorageClass change would not help. These volumes are static PVs, so the StorageClass does not apply to them.

**2. Remount the volume**
- A PV change does not touch a mount that already exists on the node. The CSI driver reads the options only when it mounts the volume.
- The node has one shared mount for the volume. Four pods use it: `sabnzbd`, `qbittorrent`, `sonarr` and `radarr`.
- All four pods must stop before the old mount is released. After Flux applies the change, I scale those four deployments to 0, wait for the unmount, then scale them back to 1. The downtime is a minute or two.
- Then I check `/proc/mounts` inside the SABnzbd pod. It must show `hard` instead of `soft`.

**Risk**
- With `hard`, the client waits for the NAS and retries without limit. SABnzbd stalls for the length of the reset. It no longer gets an error. If the NAS stays offline, processes that touch `/downloads` hang until it returns.
- The kernel log will still show the `Error -32` lines. The test is whether SABnzbd pauses again, not whether those lines disappear.

Should I make the change, commit it to `main` and do the remount? The remount interrupts running downloads and the pods for a short time.

The downloads share is now mounted `hard` with its own SMB session. SABnzbd, qBittorrent, Radarr and Sonarr are all running again.

**What changed**
- **First try:** I added `hard` to the `media-downloads` PV (commit `72f12fa1`). The mount still showed `soft`. The kernel reuses one share connection for every mount of `//nas/Media`, so the earlier `soft` mounts decided the options.
- **Fix:** I added `nosharesock` (commit `02046b76`, applied by Flux). It gives the downloads mount its own TCP session and share connection. The mount line now shows `hard` and `nosharesock`.
- **Side effect:** The kernel now reports 2 CIFS sessions. SABnzbd no longer shares a session with the Jellyfin and arr mounts. A reset of the shared session no longer hits both.
- **Downtime:** I stopped the four apps twice, about a minute each time.

**What I have not shown**
- I have not shown that this stops the pauses. The test is time. The next NAS reset should show as a short stall and not a pause.
- If a pause happens again, the `SABnzbdPaused` alert fires after 5 minutes. The NAS journal and `k8s-3` kernel logs are both in Loki for that time.
- With `hard`, a long NAS outage makes processes that touch `/downloads` hang until the NAS returns. Restarting the pod does not clear a hung mount.

**Still open**

The `hard` mount did not stop the pause. SABnzbd paused at 23:45:17 with the same `Errno 11` on `os.close(fd)`, 1.5 seconds after the NAS logged a reset of the downloads session. The mount was confirmed `hard` and `nosharesock` at that time. SABnzbd stayed paused for about 15 hours, until you resumed it at 14:59.

**What the data shows**
- **Reset:** At 23:45:16 the NAS logged `disconnect` and `connect` for `Media` and `IPC$` on the new downloads session. That session has `Instance: 2` on `k8s-3`, one reconnect since I remounted. So sharing a session was not the cause.
- **Silent client:** The `k8s-3` kernel logged no CIFS error at 23:45. The client reconnected without a message. `hard` retries failed requests, but the `close()` call still got `EAGAIN`.
- **Heavy load:** Around the reset, the NAS received 53–98 MB/s and sent up to 79 MB/s on a **1 Gbps** link. That is close to full capacity. Measured round-trip time on the SMB connections is 14–16 ms, which is high for a LAN. TCP retransmits ran at 8–46 per second. Disk, memory and CPU on the NAS were not stressed.
- **Not the cause:** The NAS had no dropped packets, no link flap, and no `smartctl_exporter` effect. The exporter was not installed when the earlier pauses happened.
- **Likely mechanism (a hypothesis):** Sustained heavy writes fill the 1 Gbps link. A send stalls, and the client drops the connection and reconnects. I have not shown this with a packet capture.

**Two things I got wrong or left open**
- The Alloy node-log parser uses `talos-time` as the timestamp. That time is about 16 minutes early. I should drop that stage and use ingestion time, so Loki lines line up with the NAS journal.
- The `SABnzbdPaused` alert should have fired at 23:50. I have not checked where alerts go. Nothing reached you, so I suspect no notification route exists.

**Options**
1. **Move `incomplete` to Longhorn (recommended).** SABnzbd would assemble and unpack on local NVMe. The NAS gets one sequential write per finished file. This matches the one workaround reported for the UNAS Pro in the [KPN thread](https://community.kpn.com/thuisnetwerk-72/linux-cifs-smb-loopt-vast-bij-langdurige-schrijfacties-naar-unas-pro-d-state-cifs-vfs-timeout-650815).
2. **Cap SABnzbd download speed** at about 70 MB/s. This is a cheap test of the saturation theory, but it does not remove the cause.
3. **Capture packets** on the NAS (`tcpdump` is installed) until the next reset. This shows which side closes the connection.

NTP is working. The skew comes from how the kernel stamps its own messages, and it is not a clock fault.

**What I measured**
- **NTP is correct:** The `k8s-3` clock differs from the NTP server by 6 ms (`talosctl time`), and `timestatus` shows `synced: true`. The NAS, the SABnzbd log and the Loki ingestion time agree within about 1.5 seconds. Examples: the NAS reset at 23:45:16 and the SABnzbd error at 23:45:17.95.
- **Boot anchor is correct:** Talos converts each kernel message time with `anchor + clock`. The anchor it uses (`2026-05-31 18:39:21Z`) matches the kernel's real boot time (`18:39:22Z` from `/proc/stat`) within 1 second.
- **Skew is in the kernel `clock` field:** The kernel stamps its messages with a raw hardware clock that NTP never adjusts. Wall time is NTP-adjusted, so the two drift apart. Over 163 days of uptime the gap is about 16 minutes. That is about 68 ppm (about 6 seconds per day), which is normal for a crystal.
- **Growth matches:** The offset was 15 min 26 s on Nov 5. It was 15 min 56 s on Nov 10. That is 30 seconds in 5 days. I measured both against the CSI driver's own log times.

**What this means**
- **Kernel lines only:** Only kernel messages (`clock` field) carry the skew. Service logs such as machined and kubelet use the wall clock when they are written, so they are accurate.
- **Grows with uptime:** The skew grows about 1 minute per 10 days of uptime. A reboot resets it to near zero.
- **The NAS shows it too:** Its uptime is 22 days, and the skew is about 2 minutes. The link-flap times I read from `dmesg` were off by that much. The Nov 8 flaps show 00:55 in `dmesg` and 00:57 in the journal.
- **Journal times are good:** The NAS journal and Alloy on the NAS use the time of receipt, so those lines are accurate.

**Fix**

Your 70 MB/s limit is a good test, and it changes what the next result means. Before the limit, the 23:45 reset came at 97–103 MB/s. Now there are two cases:

- **A pause at or below 70 MB/s.** Then link saturation is not the trigger, and the Longhorn `incomplete` volume stays the best fix.

**The persistent capture is running on the NAS**
- **Capture:** `tcpdump` keeps a ring of 12 × 128 MB files in RAM (`/dev/shm/pcap`). It holds only the first 96 bytes of each packet, for SMB traffic between `k8s-3` and the NAS. At full load it covers a few minutes.
- **Trigger:** A second service watches the NAS journal. When `k8s-3` disconnects from `Media`, it waits 3 seconds and copies the ring to `/var/lib/smb-pcap/<time>/`, with a `trigger.txt`. It keeps the last 5 events. I tested it with a fake log line, which created the copy. I then deleted the test copy.
- **Reboot behavior:** The services start at boot. The ring in RAM starts empty after a reboot. `restore-monitoring.sh` also restores them after a firmware update.
- **Cost:** The ring uses 1.5 GB of RAM, and it writes to disk only at events. About 5.7 GB of RAM stays free.

**What a capture will show**
- Whether the NAS or `k8s-3` sends the `FIN` or `RST` that ends the connection.
- Whether the TCP window went to zero in the seconds before the reset. A zero window means one side stopped reading.
- Retransmissions and stalls in the last 2–3 minutes.

## The options

| Tool | What it is | Fit for you |
|---|---|---|
| **SABnzbd** (what you run, 5.0.x) | The standard downloader. All the \*arr apps support it. | Keep it. It is actively maintained. |
| **NZBGet** | Lighter C++ downloader. The original author stopped in 2022. | **NzbDav / InfiniDysk** | A WebDAV server with a SABnzbd-compatible API. It streams from Usenet and does not download first. The project was renamed [InfiniDysk](https://nzbdav.com/), and a Rust rewrite (2.x) is in beta. | A different model. Sonarr and Radarr import through rclone symlinks or `.strm` files. |
| **AltMount** | The same idea: a [Usenet virtual filesystem](https://deepwiki.com/kipsilabs/altmount) with FUSE or rclone mounts and a SABnzbd emulator. Reported as early-stage, with a migration tool from NzbDav. | Same trade-offs as NzbDav. |

## Should you move to a streaming tool?
Probably not now.
- **Real benefit:** There is no large download, no unpack and no big write to the NAS. That removes your SMB load.
- **Costs:** Playback depends on your Usenet provider's speed and retention. There is no permanent copy on your NAS. Jellyfin reads through a WebDAV or rclone layer. Your whole media setup would change.
- **Maturity:** These projects are young, and the forks and names keep changing. Check each project's current release notes before you depend on one.

## Tuning SABnzbd for your problem
Your pauses start at the `os.close(fd)` call in SABnzbd's file assembler, in the path that takes a `direct_write` flag. I did not look up these settings, so check the names against your version's UI.
1. **Move `incomplete` to local storage.** This is still the biggest win. It stops the write, assemble and unpack traffic on SMB.
2. **Turn off Direct Unpack.** It unpacks while downloading, so reads and writes run at the same time on the share.
3. **Check the direct-write setting.** It may write each article at its final position in the file. That makes many small writes over SMB. If SABnzbd 5 lets you turn it off, try that.
4. **Raise the article cache.** More RAM for the cache means fewer small writes. The pod limit is 12 Gi, so there is room.
5. **Pause downloads during post-processing.** This lowers the overlap of heavy writes and reads.
6. **Keep the 70 MB/s limit** until the capture shows what causes the resets.

## My recommendation
Stay on SABnzbd. Fix the storage path first (item 1). If you want to try a different model later, NzbDav or AltMount could run next to SABnzbd for a small test, with a separate category in Sonarr.
